item.title: How lifestyle, late detection fuel diabetes crisis in Nigeria
item.description: As Nigeria joins the rest of the world to commemorate World Diabetes Day(WDD), marked annually on Nov. 14, health experts have warned that changing lifestyles and late detection are fuelling a diabetes crisis in the country. WDD is commemorated to raise awareness on prevention, early detection and care. Diabetes Mellitus, a chronic metabolic condition characterised by elevated blood sugar due to inability of the pancreas to produce enough insulin or impaired insulin action, has become a major public health concern, with complications including blindness, kidney failure, heart failure, stroke and limb amputation. According to the International Diabetes Federation (IDF) Diabetes Atlas, globally no fewer than 589 million adults live with diabetes, with 24.6 million in Africa. About 11 million adults live with the condition in Nigeria, with many unaware of their status. Experts said the disease, which could remain undetected for years without symptoms, was now killing more Nigerians than malaria, HIV and tuberculosis combined. An Endocrinologist, Prof. Michael Olamoyegun, said diabetes killed more Nigerians than malaria, HIV and tuberculosis combined. Olamoyegun is Professor of Medicine and Endocrinology at Ladoke Akintola University of Technology and also Consultant Physician and Endocrinologist at LAUTECH Teaching Hospital, Ogbomoso, Oyo State. He said diabetes is a metabolic disorder of carbohydrates, fats and protein. He added that it is characterised by elevated blood sugar due to inability of pancreas to produce enough insulin. According to him, diabetes also occurs if insulin action is impaired. He said there are many variants but three main types existed – Type 1, Type 2 and Gestational Diabetes. ” Type 1 diabetes, which occurs due to absolute deficiency of insulin, is seen mainly in younger age group, usually less than 30 years, although occasionally in adulthood. “It is found in about five to ten per cent of all individuals with diabetes. “This group is managed with insulin injections since the body no longer produces insulin.” The endocrinologist said Type 2 diabetes represented 90 to 95 per cent of individuals with diabetes, stressing it occurred when insulin was not able to function well in the body. He also noted that it usually occurred in older individuals who had family history in first-degree relatives. Olamoyegun, also the Secretary General of the Association of Clinical Endocrinologists of Nigeria (ACEN), added that hypertension, overweight or obesity and sedentary lifestyles were contributory risk factors. He said it is usually managed with oral medications, dietary control and occasionally with insulin. On gestational diabetes mellitus, he said it was first detected in pregnancy, saying it complicated about 7.5 to 12 per cent of all pregnancies. item.title: Airspace Now ‘Opened Up,’ No Cyberattack — US
item.description: The United States on Friday lifted an hours-long ground stop at the nation’s airports, with top officials explaining that the disruption was due to old equipment and not a cyberattack or sweeping Microsoft outage. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told a late-night briefing at the White House that US airspace was now “opened up,” while warning it would take time for the travel chaos to clear. “At 8:15 tonight Eastern Time, we’ve opened up the airspace,” Duffy said. “Now does that mean every flight is going to fly right now? It’s going to be slow.” Passengers wait for updates at a check-in area at Terminal 7 at Los Angeles International Airport, in Los Angeles on November 13, 2026. US aviation regulators issued an extremely rare ground stop of all flights across the country on November 13 after a major communications outage which the Department of Homeland Security said did not appear to be the result of any “nefarious attack.” The breakdown came a day after Duffy and the White House had formally asked Congress for $30 billion to upgrade and modernize the US Air Traffic Control System. “Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data, and they went down,” Duffy said. “It’s the old hardware that went down, and I think the question for the American people is: Do you want your Congress to fund this?” Duffy, however, insisted it was still safe for Americans to fly. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin dismissed speculation about a coordinated cyber assault on the United States, or any link to the Microsoft outage that affected services worldwide. “Welcome to Friday the 13th, right? You know, I want to make sure everybody understands that there is no connection between this and Microsoft. I know a lot of people are making that jump,” Mullin said. Mullin added there was “actually no cyber attack.” “When we start looking at cyber threats, cyber attacks, typically some people are going to raise their hand up and say, ‘Hey, we did that.’ There’s no chatter.’ We haven’t seen any footprints,” he added. But he said US security and law enforcement agencies were still checking and had ruled nothing out. Passengers wait in line to retrieve their luggage as flights were cancelled at Chicago O’Hare International Airport in Chicago on November 13, 2026. The two officials also defended President Donald Trump, who had yet to comment on the air stoppage some five hours after it began. “President Trump immediately had people in his office,” Mullin said. “We were communicating.” Passengers wait at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, Washington, DC on November 13, 2026. item.title: APC Women Target 10 Million Votes For Tinubu In 2027
item.description: The Women Mobilisation Committee of the All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council has pledged to mobilise 10 million women’s votes nationwide for President Bola Tinubu in the 2027 general elections. The pledge was made by the APC National Women Leader and Director of the Women Mobilisation Committee of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, Mary Alile Idele, at a town hall meeting held in Gusau on Thursday. Addressing women leaders, party stakeholders and supporters from across the 14 local government areas of Zamfara State, Idele urged women to deliver massive votes for President Tinubu in recognition of the impact of his administration on their lives. She acknowledged what she described as the Tinubu administration’s achievements in transforming the lives of Nigerian women and their children, saying the government had deliberately placed women at the centre of its Renewed Hope Agenda. APC Women target 10 million votes for Tinubu in 2027 According to her, the President has demonstrated a strong commitment to women’s empowerment through policies and programmes that directly impact women in both rural and urban communities. She identified the Student Loan Scheme as one of the administration’s landmark achievements, noting that it had provided many Nigerian children, including those from disadvantaged families in Zamfara, with opportunities to pursue higher education without the burden of tuition fees. Idele also highlighted women’s empowerment initiatives, including cash grants, which she said had enabled thousands of women to establish and expand small businesses, support their families and achieve greater economic independence. She added that the distribution of starter packs to trained women had helped beneficiaries apply their acquired skills immediately, rather than returning home without the necessary tools to start their businesses. The APC National Women Leader further commended the administration’s support for women in agriculture, explaining that female farmers in Zamfara and other states had benefited from farm inputs, training and other interventions aimed at boosting food production and improving their income. Also speaking at the town hall meeting, the wife of the Director-General of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, Hajiya Asmau Yari, described the visit of First Lady Senator Oluremi Tinubu to Zamfara as historic and heartwarming. She said Mrs Tinubu was the first Nigerian First Lady to visit Zamfara State since its creation, describing the visit as a demonstration of love, respect and recognition for the women of the state. Asmau Yari urged Zamfara women to reciprocate the gesture by voting massively for President Tinubu in the 2027 general elections to enable him to consolidate on the gains already recorded by his administration. item.title: 2027: Gov Eno Unveils Arise 2.0 Manifesto, Inaugurates APC State Campaign Council
item.description: Akwa Ibom State Governor, Pastor Umo Eno, has unveiled his manifesto and development blueprint for a proposed second term, tagged ARISE 2.0, promising more ambitious projects and a stronger focus on economic growth, investment, tourism, agriculture and job creation. He unveiled the blueprint during the inauguration of the All Progressives Congress (APC) State Campaign Council ahead of the 2027 general elections, describing the occasion as a defining moment in the state’s development journey. Anchoring the campaign on the theme, “We Are Well Able,” drawn from Numbers 13:30, Eno said Akwa Ibom had the capacity to achieve greater development milestones and improve the living conditions of its people. Reflecting on his administration’s performance since May 29, 2023, Governor Eno said the ARISE Agenda had provided a foundation for progress in infrastructure, education, healthcare, agriculture, housing, rural development, tourism and youth empowerment. He explained that ARISE 2.0 would build on the achievements of the first phase, with a shift from an infrastructure-driven economy towards a more productive economy anchored on investment, enterprise and private-sector participation. On economic expansion, Eno promised to strengthen the business environment, attract local and foreign investors, support entrepreneurs and create more opportunities for private-sector growth. He also identified tourism as a major driver of the state’s economic transformation, saying Akwa Ibom would leverage its natural attractions, cultural heritage, hospitality, culinary traditions and geographical advantages to become a destination for conferences, entertainment, holidays, sports and cultural festivals. As part of plans to transform Uyo’s urban landscape, Governor Eno announced the proposed remodelling of the city centre, featuring an iconic tower, flyover and other facilities, saying the capital city would have a significantly changed skyline. In agriculture, he pledged a transition from subsistence farming to commercial production and agro-industrialisation through modern farming techniques, farm settlements, increased support for farmers and expanded agro-processing activities. He also promised continued investment in roads, electricity, transportation and public infrastructure, alongside improvements in education, healthcare, technical training and skills acquisition. On youth development, Governor Eno said young people must become active participants and beneficiaries of the emerging economy through empowerment, entrepreneurship and employment opportunities. He added that social protection would remain central to his administration, particularly for senior citizens, persons living with disabilities and vulnerable families. Addressing the proposed Ibom Deep Seaport, Eno described the project as a strategic component of the state’s long-term economic ambition. He appreciated President Bola Tinubu for his support, following recent progress in the project’s certification

item.title: Tight security as Tinubu visits Jos for APC presidential rally
item.description: By Golok Nanmwa, Jos Security has been beefed up in Jos, the Plateau State capital, ahead of the expected arrival of President Bola Tinubu on Saturday for the All Progressives Congress (APC) North-Central presidential campaign rally. Our correspondent, who visited several parts of the city, observed a heavy deployment of security personnel at strategic locations, including Hill Station Junction, Zaria Road, Polo Roundabout and parts of Yakubu Gowon Way, as security agencies intensified surveillance ahead of the President’s visit. Tinubu is expected to attend the APC presidential rally scheduled to hold at the Zaria Road Stadium, Jos, where he is also expected to commission three major development projects executed by the Plateau State Government. The projects are the Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) Centre in Jos, the Plateau Special Activity Centre (P-SAC) and 50 hybrid Jet Mover buses for inter-local government transportation. Ahead of the President’s visit, Governor Caleb Mutfwang, APC National Chairman, Professor Nentawe Yilwatda, and former Deputy Governor, Dame Pauline Tallen, inspected the facilities. Speaking on the BPO Centre, Mutfwang described it as a strategic investment in human capital development, job creation and economic empowerment. According to a statement signed by his Director of Press and Public Affairs, Gyang Bere, the governor said the facility, established through a partnership between the Plateau State Government, Outsource Global and MTN Nigeria, has an operational capacity of 800 seats and is projected to generate up to 2,400 direct full-time jobs when fully deployed across three shifts. He said the centre would connect Plateau youths to the global digital economy through customer experience management, technical support and back-office services. Mutfwang added that young people would be able to work for international organisations from Jos and earn in foreign currencies. On the Plateau Special Activity Centre, the governor said the facility was established to strengthen intelligence-driven security operations, stressing that security remained fundamental to sustainable development. The centre comprises a Fusion and Analytical Centre, Geo-Intelligence/GIS Unit, Drone Unit, Training Centre and Profiling Room to enhance intelligence gathering, threat detection, analysis and coordinated security responses. He also said the 50 hybrid buses would improve public transportation, reduce travel costs and enhance connectivity across the state’s 17 local government areas. Meanwhile, during an inspection of the Zaria Road Stadium, venue of the rally, Mutfwang expressed confidence that the event would attract massive participation from APC supporters and stakeholders across the North-Central region. He urged residents to turn out in large numbers to welcome Tinubu, whom he described as a statesman committed to the development and security of Plateau State. item.title: ABSU VC bans birthday parties, awards, courtesy visits
item.description: By Steve Oko UMUAHIA — The newly-appointed Vice-Chancellor of Abia State University, ABSU, Uturu, Prof. Amadike Ugbogu, has banned courtesy visits by faculties and departments, birthday celebrations, award presentations and portrait gifts in his honour throughout his tenure. Read Also: (Video) UNN Party Tragedy: How I regained consciousness, found friends lying lifeless – Survivor The directive, contained in a notice issued by the University’s Media and Public Relations Unit, also prohibits the acceptance of birthday cakes and honours from individuals, organisations, churches and communities. Prof. Ugbogu appreciated the university community for the goodwill and support accorded him during his inauguration. But directed faculties and departments to discontinue courtesy visits to his office. Rather than receive delegations, the Vice-Chancellor said he would personally visit the various faculties and departments to interact with staff and acquaint himself with their activities, achievements and challenges. He also made it clear that he would not entertain birthday parties organised in his honour or accept birthday cakes. The university community, students, staff and members of the public were urged to respect and cooperate with the directives. The Vice-Chancellor who assumed office barely two weeks ago, reaffirmed his commitment to purposeful leadership, academic excellence, institutional development and the overall progress of the university. item.title: Argentina beaten by Uruguay in first game since Messi retirement
item.description: Argentina suffered a 2-1 defeat against Uruguay on Friday in their first game since Lionel Messi’s retirement from international football. A second-half own goal by Argentina defender Leonardo Balerdi followed by a fluky effort from Uruguay midfielder Maxi Araujo sealed defeat for the 2026 World Cup runners-up. Atletico Madrid striker Julian Alavarez gave Argentina hope of a comeback with a 73rd-minute strike but Uruguay held on to clinch a third victory for new manager Diego Forlan. Messi played his final game for Argentina in an emotional farewell friendly victory over Benin last month, calling time on a glittering career that spanned 207 caps and 125 goals. With the 39-year-old genius missing, Argentina struggled to break down a resilient Uruguay team for long stretches of Friday’s friendly. Nico Paz had Argentina’s best chance of the first half, but saw his shot well-saved by Uruguay goalkeeper Cristopher Fiermarin. Uruguay made the breakthrough soon after half-time when a Giorgian de Arrascaeta free-kick from the left caused chaos in the Argentina defence. Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez attempted to clear with a header but his effort instead cannoned off team-mate Balerdi and into the net. De Arrascaeta then set up Uruguay’s second in the 53rd minute, his corner appearing to hit Araujo’s shoulder before looping high into the net. Alvarez pulled a goal back midway through the half, and had another good chance in stoppage time but Uruguay closed out the win. item.title: Hundreds of million for 90 minutes, peanuts for a lifetime of service, by Stephanie Shaakaa
item.description: *Nigeria’s Broken Scale of Value When the Super Falcons clinched their record-extending tenth Women’s Africa Cup of Nations title in July 2025, the Presidency rolled out the red carpet. The players received national honours, three-bedroom apartments in Abuja and the promise of the naira equivalent of $100,000 each. The financial rewards were eventually fulfilled in November 2026. Barely had that celebration settled when another Nigerian women’s team made history. The Flamingos conquered the world, becoming the first African country to win the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup. Once again, the presidential purse swung open: ₦100 million for each player, secured in savings certificates because of their young age, ₦100 million in cash for the coach and ₦50 million for each member of the technical crew. The Senate also announced a separate ₦100 million reward. Let us be clear: nobody begrudges these young girls their glory. They trained hard, carried the green-and-white flag with pride and earned their moment in the sun. Their achievement deserves recognition, and the decision to preserve their rewards in savings instruments rather than hand enormous sums directly to teenagers is commendable. The problem is not that the government rewards sporting excellence. It is what the speed, scale and enthusiasm of these announcements reveal about the Nigerian state’s priorities. There is a disturbing arithmetic to our national life: hundreds of millions for 90 minutes of football, and peanuts, sometimes outright silence, for a lifetime of service. See the contrast in Abuja. When a trophy arrives at the Presidential Villa, the government can announce substantial financial commitments, organise receptions and put together carefully structured reward packages. Even the decision to protect the Flamingos’ money through savings certificates demonstrates an ability to think ahead and make financial arrangements in the interest of young beneficiaries. Yet, outside the celebratory atmosphere of the Villa, citizens encounter a different government, one that appears to require endless negotiations, industrial threats and public agitation before certain obligations receive the attention they deserve. The contrast extends beyond workers and pensioners. Consider the survivors of the Yelewata massacre in Benue State. Having lost family members, homes and livelihoods to violence, many displaced residents continue to struggle with food, healthcare, decent shelter and other basic necessities. Investigations into conditions in Benue’s displacement camps have documented irregular food distribution, inadequate sanitation, poor healthcare facilities and families struggling to secure even one proper meal a day. These are Nigerians whose lives have been shattered by violence. They are not asking for presidential honours or millions in savings certificates. item.title: Do you think your woman is having an affair?
item.description: By Bunmi Sofola Here, a marriage counselor who has spent 16 years sifting through the ruins of other people’s relationships, gives his analysis of how a partnership can lose its way, and a few suggestions for not letting it happen. (a) Signs she is having an affair Look for a sudden short-term drop-off sex: Everyone has appetites – exactly where is she satisfying hers? Radically different sexual behavior: If she suddenly starts suggesting things he hasn’t done before, or doing things every differently even if it’s better, where is she getting the ideas from? Sudden increase in working hours: This can easily be innocent, but where’s the extra cash? (You might never know if lover boy is giving her over-time pay!) Sexually transmitted infections: Towels and toilet seat explanations simply aren’t good enough. (b) Things she is getting from an affair that she is not getting at home Excitement that is the main thing. Having a secret life. If you are clever enough, your marriage should be her secret life! (c) Full time attention He is trying harder than you. Usually a stop up, someone better than the husband in at least one respect – looks, money, youth. (d) Mistakes husbands make Not adjusting to the fact that you are married. Like it or not, you are now part of a double act, and you can’t carry on as if nothing’s happened. Women like to see visible signs of commitment, so cut down on after work drinks with the boys. (e) Getting Fat It sounds harsh, but there are a lot of thin guys out there who’ll be trying if on your wife. (f) Taking her for granted Undervaluing her, expecting her to be there and expecting her not to get suspicious when you’re having affairs. (f) Over-working A lot of high-achieving guys drive themselves hard often thinking it is for sake of their wives or family. But putting in excessive hours to generate your wealth just provides her with motive, means and opportunity for adultery. However, painful, there comes a time when a marriage is beyond repair, continues the counselor. According to him, Violence is not a good sign”. Some relationships survive it, but it’s always a black mark, never to be forgotten. It happens to the men more than you’d think; big, strong men sometimes, they just don’t defend themselves against their violent wives. (g) Child Abuse Again mainly perpetrated by men, but occasionally women. “If she’s with someone clearly out of your league. If she’s that ruthlessly upwardly mobile, you’ve had it. “If addictions are involved: Gambling, drinking, drugs, whatever, it blocks everything else out and people get pushed away past their limits … Finally, you’re to remember that when your relationship is threatened, you must spend more time away from the environment. item.title: ‘I May Lose My Mind’, Frustrated Travellers React To US Flight Havoc
item.description: Confusion reigned at airports across the United States on Friday as a rare grounding of all US flights stranded hundreds of thousands of frustrated travellers. In New York’s busy LaGuardia airport, Janice Llewellyn was on the verge of tears: the chaos could mean she will miss her daughter’s wedding in Toronto. The 61-year-old Llewellyn was desperate to find an alternative route, telling AFP: “I may lose my mind.” “My husband flew all the way from England to get to the wedding,” she said. “Oh gosh! I wish they had another flight, I wish I could get another flight, like, now.” At the airport in Las Vegas, some fliers were told their journeys were delayed due to wind. One airline staffer said the ground stop would last eight hours. Another said 24 hours. Passengers wait for updates at a check-in area at Terminal 7 at Los Angeles International Airport, in Los Angeles on November 13, 2026. US aviation regulators issued an extremely rare ground stop of all flights across the country on November 13 after a major communications outage, which the Department of Homeland Security said did not appear to be the result of any “nefarious attack.” Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) officials eventually lifted the ground stop at 8:15 pm ET (0115 GMT Saturday). “It will take us time (to) resume normal operations,” Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said, blaming the incident on telecommunications issues with decades-old equipment. During the stop, the lack of information led many passengers to form long lines at rental car counters in a mad dash for travel alternatives. Joseph Anderson said he was trying to get back to Oakland in California from Las Vegas and was considering driving — but said “if the whole country is stopped, that means the highways are going to be jammed too.” The 72-year-old retired Air Force veteran said his already-checked luggage was captive, meaning “we’re kind of stuck.” “I would hope the communication can be better from the FAA,” he said. Passengers wait in line to retrieve their luggage as flights were cancelled at Chicago O’Hare International Airport in Chicago on November 13, 2026. Friday 13th The ground stop comes less than two weeks before the Thanksgiving holiday, the busiest travel period of the year in the United States. And it falls ahead of a particularly busy weekend for professional and college sports — teams and their fans are also stuck. Back in New York, Tiara Johnson had been heading to Orlando in Florida for a weekend concert, and any hope that she would make it was growing dim. “You think you’re gonna be there in three hours, but your whole evening is kind of done!” the 50-year-old told AFP. “But hey, they say it’s Friday the 13th!” Planes sit idle at Los Angeles International Airport in Los Angeles on November 13, 2026. item.title: Trump, Xi, Putin to hold historic meeting in China – White House
item.description: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping will hold the first ever three-way meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China at a summit in Shenzhen next week, the White House said Friday. Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear arsenals at the trilateral talks on Thursday and is also set to bring up his war in Iran — but he is not expected to discuss Russia’s war in Ukraine, US officials said. The three leaders will meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese city, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters. “The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous,” Wales said. One of the major conflicts dominating Trump’s second term as president will feature, but the other will not, the US officials said. “I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin,” a senior US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call. Washington has a “whole other track” of negotiations with Kyiv and Moscow aimed at ending the war in Ukraine, the official added, referring to talks that US envoys have had in recent days with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. “China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there,” the official added. Tesla and Space X boss Elon Musk will accompany Trump on his trip to China but won’t be involved in the meeting with Xi and Putin, the officials said. Trump will also hold a bilateral working lunch and meeting with the Chinese president on Thursday — their fourth meeting since the US president’s return to power last year. But Trump is not scheduled to have a separate one-on-one with Putin. Among other topics, Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang’s resignation over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy is not expected to come up in Trump’s meetings with Xi, the officials said. “The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip,” a second US senior official said. The United States also did not plan to discuss export controls on sensitive chip technology, which were at the heart of the Nvidia scandal. “We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration… and we don’t expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we’re there,” the second official said. Trump will leave Washington on Monday and arrive in the Philippines on Tuesday for a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit before heading to Shenzhen. item.title: ‘A moral red line’? World on cusp of autonomous weapons revolution
item.description: Lethal autonomous weapons powered by artificial intelligence are set to revolutionise warfare but there is no proper regulatory or legal framework governing the new technology. Read Also: 6,000 Flight Cancelled: US air travel resumption will ‘take time’ A conference starting Monday at the United Nations in Geneva will discuss how to establish curbs and prohibitions on such weapons, called killer robots by some. But some analysts doubt the discussions at the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) will keep pace with the fast-changing weapons. AFP looks at three key questions ahead of the conference. What are LAWS? Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS) “can identify, select, and engage a target without the intervention of a human operator in the execution of these tasks,” said Jean-Marc Rickli, head of global and emerging risks at the Geneva Centre for Security Policy. Autonomous weapons have long existed. An anti-personnel mine “is an autonomous weapon in the sense that it explodes when someone steps on it,” said Laure de Roucy-Rochegonde of the Centre for Geopolitics of Technology at the French Institute of International Relations (IFRI). But with the proliferation of AI-enhanced drones, such weapons are now “capable of selecting and engaging a target that was not predetermined, adapting to their environment without human intervention,” said Rickli. So the critical issue for potential regulators lies in determining the level of human control over the decision to employ such a weapon. The United States refers to an “appropriate levels of human judgement” in the use of autonomous weapons. France maintains that a human must remain in the decision-making loop and bans “lethal autonomous weapons systems” (LAWS) but permits “partially autonomous” systems known as PLAWS. “The human role is always ensured through what is termed ‘appropriate control’ by a military commander — a concept that varies in scope depending on the system’s criticality and the operational context,” said Rear Admiral Vincent Sebastien, deputy director of the French defence ministry’s Agency for Defence Artificial Intelligence (AMIAD). The ethical issues? “We are now dangerously close to crossing a moral red line: the autonomous targeting of humans by machines,” UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, and International Committee of the Red Cross president Mirjana Spoljaric warned in a joint statement in August. But analysts said the Geneva discussions, while important, will touch only part of the issue. Today, the diminishing role of humans is being driven by the growing use of AI in analysis and targeting. Rickli said the scope of the agenda in Geneva is “very narrow”. “It fails to encompass the full range of issues surrounding AI on the battlefield” – an area where its use is expanding, particularly in target generation. item.title: 2027: Nigerians need relief now, not promises of future gains — Lamido
item.description: By Juliet Umeh Former Jigawa State Governor, Sule Lamido, has said Nigerians need to see improvements in their lives now, rather than being asked to wait for promised future gains from government policies. Read Also: Sacking of Atiku: What Justice Lifu based his judgement on Lamido, who spoke on Channels Television, said voters wanted security and the benefits of a good life in the present. “Why should I be told to wait for the future? What are you offering people now to make sure that tomorrow they believe?” he asked. “People today need to be very, very confident. But when you are saying, ‘Tomorrow, tomorrow, tomorrow,’ no, please give it to me today. I don’t want to follow you tomorrow.” The former governor also denied endorsing President Bola Tinubu for the 2027 presidential election, saying he remained committed to the Peoples Democratic Party, PDP. Lamido said: “I am PDP through and through. I’m voting for PDP. My candidate is Prof. Ono. That’s my candidate for PDP.” He said his support for the party extended to elections at all levels, including councillorship, chairmanship and governorship. Asked about reports that the PDP would work with Tinubu under a proposed “Rainbow Coalition”, Lamido said he had not been consulted about the arrangement. “He never called me, never invited me, never consulted me. So I have no idea what he is doing,” he said, referring to the party leader associated with the initiative. Lamido said he was not aware of the details of the proposed political arrangement and had not met the leader in recent months. On the 2027 campaigns, he urged candidates to focus on the country’s most pressing challenges, particularly insecurity and the economy, and explain how they planned to address them. “What are the issues in Nigeria? Security issues in the economy, these are the main issues,” he said. Lamido said voters should assess candidates by their capacity, authority, commitment and willingness to act, rather than by political alliances or rhetoric. He also warned that hate speech and divisive campaigning could deepen tensions, urging politicians to focus on what they could offer Nigerians. “The campaign should be on issues: what can you offer?” he said, criticising campaigns that dwell on personalities and division. Asked who he believed voters should support, Lamido said he was uncertain about the choices before them. “When you go in there, say, ‘God, please guide me,’ because I’m confused. I don’t know who to vote for,” he said, before reiterating his support for the PDP candidate. Lamido said the country’s unity, security and economic wellbeing should remain central to the political debate, regardless of which candidate wins the election. item.title: 6,000 Flight Cancelled: US air travel resumption will ‘take time’
item.description: Flights in the United States were resuming on Saturday after being grounded for several hours due to a major communications outage, though authorities said returning to normal operations would take time. The nationwide stop on Friday sparked widespread chaos and left hundreds of thousands of passengers in limbo, with some pulled off planes moments before departure by airline staff who appeared in the dark about unfolding events. The incident marked only the second time such an alert had been issued in US airspace — which is among the busiest in the world — since the 9/11 attacks. The ground stop lasted around four hours and was lifted at 8:15 pm Eastern Time (0115 GMT Saturday). Federal Aviation Administration officials reopened the airspace on Friday night “after restoring full functionality” at air traffic control facilities, according to Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy. “It will take us time (to) resume normal operations… Our top priority is the safety of you and your family when you fly,” Duffy said. Administration officials blamed the incident on telecommunications issues with decades-old equipment, adding there was no evidence of foul play. “This is a legacy system problem,” Duffy said. “We have old, old switches, old routers. “We use 1980s little copper lines. It’s an old system that went down, and went down everywhere. It got overloaded.” Duffy had formally asked Congress on Thursday for $30.1 billion in funds to upgrade and modernize the air traffic control System. As the ground stop was lifted, he repeated his plea. “I’m going to say it a million times: the Congress has to give the resources to the president so he can finish this bill,” he said. 6,000 flights canceled There were almost 6,000 flights canceled, including some international routes, according to FlightAware, a tracking platform. Footage from airports around the country showed gates full, with planes waiting on taxiways. Passengers thronged concourses, desperate for information about an outage that had thrown their plans into chaos. “We’re trying to debate whether or not we need to reschedule or drive or what, but if the whole country is stopped, that means the highways are going to be jammed too,” said Joseph Anderson, 72, who was trying to fly from Las Vegas to Oakland, California. A nationwide ground stop is highly unusual. There was one such stop in January 2023 when a pilot notification system failed, but the only other national stop happened in the wake of the 9/11 attacks in September 2001, when no aircraft took to the skies for days. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin stressed there was no evidence of any hostile action on Friday. “We’ve seen zero evidence that this was a cyberattack or (AI) attack,” he told a news conference. He also ruled out any connection with the outage that affected Microsoft this week, knocking email systems offline for millions of users, public services and businesses worldwide. item.title: Delta 2027: Omo-Agege challenging political establishment he helped to build
item.description: By Egufe Yafugborhi For a politician who once occupied the number three position in Nigeria’s constitutional order, served two terms in the Senate and declared that he had completed his legislative assignment, Senator Ovie Omo-Agege’s decision to seek a return to the Red Chamber presents an intriguing twist in Delta State’s changing political history. More intriguing is his choice of Delta Central, the district he represented for eight years. He is now facing Senator Ede Dafinone, the incumbent he helped bring into the Senate in 2023, but who now belongs to the political establishment that has taken over the party Omo-Agege once controlled in Delta. It is a contest laden with political irony, bruised relationships and competing ambitions, raising questions about whether personal political capital can survive the collapse of an established political structure. Today, Omo-Agege is seeking a Senate return on the platform of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), while Dafinone remains the APC incumbent, backed by a party now accommodating much of Delta’s former PDP political establishment. From Ibori’s government to the Senate Omo-Agege’s political journey has taken him through government, opposition politics and national legislative influence. A lawyer, he began his major political career under former Governor James Ibori, serving as Executive Assistant, Commissioner for Special Duties and later Secretary to the Delta State Government between 2003 and 2007. After leaving government, he returned to private business and political mobilisation, eventually emerging as senator representing Delta Central in 2015. His re-election in 2019 elevated his stature further. He became Deputy President of the Ninth Senate, placing him among the most influential political officeholders from the Niger Delta. But in 2023, he abandoned the familiar senatorial contest to challenge for the governorship under the APC against Sheriff Oborevwori, the PDP candidate and successor to former Governor Ifeanyi Okowa. It was a bruising contest that divided political loyalties across Delta. Oborevwori eventually polled 360,234 votes against Omo-Agege’s 240,229, ending his immediate governorship ambition but not his political relevance. The Political Tsunami And The Lost Territory The defining rupture came in 2025. Before Oborevwori and Okowa moved into the APC, Omo-Agege openly challenged their proposed entry. At an APC stakeholders’ engagement in February, he declared that the two leaders had no moral ground to abandon the PDP, a party they had repeatedly described as insurmountable in Delta. He insisted they should remain in the PDP and rebuild the structure they had once celebrated. He argued that the APC had already established itself in Delta, winning two senatorial seats and other legislative positions in 2023, and did not need the wholesale arrival of politicians who had spent years presenting the PDP as unbeatable. item.title: 2027: Presidential choice exposes widening elite-grassroots divide in South-East
item.description: By Steve Oko, Regional Editor, South East The scene at the School of Health Aba, the commercial capital of Abia State last weekend offered a fascinating glimpse into what could become one of the defining political contradictions of the 2027 presidential election. It showed the widening gulf between the political calculations of South East power brokers and the apparent preferences of the ordinary people. It was a moment when political establishment encountered popular sentiment, and the response from the crowd was anything but pretence. The masses, in unmistakable terms, passed a strong message: they are not in for jokes! They know what is good for them. While a significant section of the South East political establishment, including governors, National Assembly members and other influential politicians, has either openly or tacitly aligned with President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s re-election ambition, the grassroots appear to be gravitating in a different direction, with the former Anambra State governor, and the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, flag bearer, Mr Peter Obi, retaining a formidable following across the region. The drama unfolded when Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, Rt. Hon. Benjamin Kalu, attended the 2026 Item Day organised by the Item people in Aba. Kalu hails from Bende town, a neighbouring community with Item. As a prominent supporter of President Tinubu, Kalu apparently saw the gathering as an opportunity to canvass support for the President ahead of 2027. He never wanted to miss the opportunity, and rightly so. But what followed was a political moment he might not have anticipated. He never dreamed of the dramatic turn of events as he grabbed the microphone to market Tinubu’s candidacy. Dressed in the traditional Igbo (isiagu) attire, with a red cap to match, Kalu who prides himself as ‘the number six’ man in the country, mounted the stage and urged the people to support Tinubu’s re-election, assuring them that the President would do more for Abia if given another mandate. ‘Tinubu’ to ‘Obi kererenke’ “Tinubu will do more for Abia. Vote for Tinubu in 2027. He is the best for Nigeria,” he told the gathering. But as the Deputy Speaker shouted “Tinubu”, apparently expecting an enthusiastic response from the crowd, what came back was a thunderous rendition of “Obi kererenke”, the popular solidarity chant associated with Peter Obi. The response was spontaneous, collective and blunt! Even with a microphone, Kalu’s voice appeared drowned by the surging chants of the crowd. Attempts to calm the gathering did little to change the mood. Neither his assurance of a proposed federal university for Item nor the intervention of a performing artiste, who quickly introduced another Tinubu campaign song, “On Your Mandate We Shall Stand”, could dislodge the crowd’s enthusiasm for Obi. item.title: Tinubu’s aide dismisses claims of convoy stoning
item.description: O’tega Ogra, Senior Special Assistant to President Bola Tinubu on Digital Engagement, Strategy and New Media, has disputed claims that the president’s convoy was attacked by youths following his attendance at Friday prayers at the Shagari Central Mosque in Area 1, Abuja. Tinubu had visited the mosque in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) for the Juma’at prayer on Friday. However, Dino Melaye, a chieftain of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), later shared a video showing some youths throwing stones at a convoy believed to belong to the president. In the video, which has circulated widely on social media, some of the youths were heard chanting, “Ba ma yi, ba ma so”, a Hausa expression meaning “we don’t want you; we don’t support you”. Reacting to the development, Ogra shared a separate video showing Tinubu leaving the mosque after the prayers. “Contrary to the narrative being pushed by the opposition, with videos of their alleged paid thugs at the National Mosque today, here is footage of Mr President leaving the mosque after Friday prayers this afternoon,” Ogra wrote. The footage showed Tinubu, dressed in a white outfit and black cap, waving to youths who cheered him and took photographs with their mobile phones as he made his way into his official vehicle. Ogra’s response challenged the account circulating on social media. However, the footage he shared did not independently establish whether the incident captured in Melaye’s video occurred at another location along the president’s route. The development comes amid growing concerns over political violence ahead of the 2027 general election. In a statement he personally signed on Friday, Tinubu warned politicians and their supporters against resorting to violence, saying security agencies had been authorised to deal decisively with thuggery and other anti-democratic activities. He condemned reported incidents of violence at political events across the country and urged political actors to focus their campaigns on issues affecting the welfare of Nigerians and national development. The president reiterated that violence had no place in political campaigns. The post Tinubu’s aide dismisses claims of convoy stoning appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: What has changed for Asaba since Azinge became Asagba?
item.description: By Egufe Yafugborhi When HRM Prof. Epiphany Chigbogu Azinge, SAN, ascended the throne of the Asagba of Asaba two years ago, he inherited an institution steeped in history, tradition and expectations. Today, the palace is becoming something more. A smart school has been built by the community and handed to the Delta State Government. Ambulances respond to emergencies. A drug rehabilitation centre has emerged. Security intelligence flows into the palace within minutes. Public spaces are being upgraded, a 1000-capacity Event Centre hosted guests to Nna Agu’s second coronation anniversary. Women are gaining a stronger voice in traditional affairs. Even long-standing practices such as community burials are being reviewed. For Azinge, the change is deliberate. He declared, “I’ve long migrated from being a traditional ruler, and now into traditional governance. I’m not only trying to think about the customs and traditions of our people. “I’m also thinking about the welfare, healthcare, education, among so many other things, to make sure my people, Asaba people, collectively, are very happy going forward.” It is a philosophy beginning to redefine what many residents expect from their traditional institution, the people building for themselves Perhaps nowhere is the new relationship between palace and people more visible than at the Asaba Community Smart Nursery And Primary School recently commissioned and donated by Asaba to the Delta State Government. Asagba Azinge sees it more than a building. “Today, Asaba is breaking new grounds. We try to shatter ceilings, if and when the opportunity presents itself. “I believe in the history of Delta state, and I dare say of Nigeria, this is the first time a community will come together, not just to build a smart school, but also have it donated to government” The project, he said, demonstrates that the traditional institution can mobilise the community while government provides the broader public-service framework. “It underscores our willingness, readiness at all times to partner our state government, complement their efforts, and support them in the growth and development of our state and our community in particular.” But the partnership comes with expectations. Standing at the school, Azinge turned to the government with a simple request: “If Asaba can donate a school to you, please donate a road to us so we can achieve this. Donate a road so people can access this place easily and then be able to school here.” For Delta State Commissioner for Primary Education, Chief Mrs Rose Ezewu, the message was equally clear. “This occasion is significant not merely because we are unveiling a new school facility, but because we are witnessing the power of community vision, responsible leadership and purposeful partnership in advancing the cause of education. “Sustainable progress requires collaboration with communities, traditional institutions, parents and other stakeholders.” A Palace That Listens If the school represent

item.title: Why 16 Nigerians died transiting through Addis Ababa
item.description: By Favour Ulebor, Abuja The Federal Government has advised Nigerians, particularly those with underlying health conditions, to exercise caution when travelling through Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, following the death of 16 Nigerians in the city this year. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued the advisory on Friday, revealing that Nigeria’s diplomatic mission in Addis Ababa recorded 16 deaths involving Nigerians transiting through the Ethiopian capital. The deaths were reportedly linked to health complications associated with the city’s high altitude. According to the ministry, Addis Ababa is located about 2,355 metres (7,726 feet) above sea level, where lower atmospheric pressure results in reduced oxygen levels. The ministry noted that while most healthy individuals can adapt to such conditions, travellers with pre-existing cardiovascular or respiratory illnesses may face increased health risks. “This year, Nigeria’s Diplomatic Mission in Addis Ababa has recorded 16 deaths involving Nigerians transiting through the city, reportedly linked to health complications associated with high altitude,” the statement said. The government therefore urged Nigerians whose medical conditions could be worsened by high-altitude environments to seek medical advice before travelling through Addis Ababa. “Travellers with underlying medical conditions are strongly advised to obtain appropriate medical guidance before undertaking such journeys,” the ministry stated However, the Federal Government stressed that the advisory was not intended to discourage Nigerians from travelling to or transiting through Addis Ababa. “Rather, it aims to ensure that persons who may be medically vulnerable to the physiological effects of high altitudes are adequately informed and encouraged to take necessary precautions,” the statement added. The ministry reaffirmed the government’s commitment to safeguarding the health, safety and wellbeing of Nigerians abroad through timely travel advisories and other consular support measures. item.title: Egemen Mustafa Şener on the three words he learned in a Black Sea village that still run his business
item.description: Çifteköprü is a small village in the Borçka district of Artvin, in Türkiye’s Eastern Black Sea region. It is the kind of place where the weather decides more of the week than any calendar does, where a neighbour’s word carries the same weight as a document, and where the ground gives back exactly what the work put in. It is also where Egemen Mustafa Şener learned, before he ever ran a construction site in Istanbul or a shipyard project in Montevideo, the three practices that still organise his business today. The three words, as the company itself frames them, are labor, promises, and land. From a Black Sea farm to an Istanbul construction site Şener was born in Çifteköprü in May 1968. His father worked the land, his mother came from a well-established Laz family, and the household ran on a set of unspoken rules that any rural community would recognise. Work was visible or it hadn’t happened. A spoken commitment was binding. The land did not reward shortcuts. When he moved to Istanbul after high school, into business school and then into agricultural trading in the late 1980s, those rules didn’t get left behind. By the early 1990s, when he had shifted into residential and commercial construction and was managing his first sites in the city, the same three practices were doing the actual work of running the business. The language of the construction industry was new, but the habits underneath it were the same ones he had grown up with. Egemen Mustafa Şener on labor, in a sector where everything has to be seen The first of the three is labor, and in construction it is not a metaphor. Every person on a site contributes something that is either visible in the finished work or hidden inside it. A good site manager is one who can see the work that is supposed to be hidden as clearly as the work on the surface. Visible labor is also what makes delivery possible. A project is a stack of promises about what will happen on which date, and every one of those promises rests on someone actually doing the work. When labor becomes abstract, delivery slips. In three decades of residential, commercial, industrial and infrastructure projects, this has not changed. The promise that does the work before the contract does The second word is promises. In most business settings, promises are secondary to contracts. In the one Egemen Mustafa Şener grew up in, they were the contract. A spoken commitment was held because the alternative, in a village the size of Çifteköprü, was impossible to live with. Transplanted into construction, that habit becomes a working style. A contract will specify the delivery date and the quality standard. But between any two reasonable parties, the real agreement is the one that was given before the paperwork caught up, and the business that honours that version tends to finish projects on terms that match what was actually said. item.title: Lumumba identifies what’s fueling xenophobia
item.description: •Says Africa cannot fight poverty by turning against fellow Africans Professor Patrick Loch Otieno (PLO) Lumumba has warned that Africa’s failure to create sufficient economic opportunities is fuelling xenophobia. He urged governments to address unemployment, poverty and weak industrial development rather than blame migrants for the continent’s challenges. Lumumba, a renowned Kenyan legal scholar and public speaker, said xenophobia often thrived in societies experiencing economic hardship, where unemployment, inequality and pressure on public services encouraged citizens to regard foreigners as competitors. He spoke as the keynote speaker at the Bridge Club’s grand end-of-year event in Lagos on Thursday. In his address, titled Africa Must Not Become Foreign to Itself: Xenophobia, Pan-Africanism and the Future of African Belonging, Lumumba argued that migrants were frequently made scapegoats for economic problems arising from poor governance and weak institutions. He said: “The foreign trader, worker or entrepreneur can be arrested. The failure to create productive employment over several decades cannot be arrested at a roadblock.” According to him, African governments must look beyond the presence of migrants and examine the structural weaknesses responsible for unemployment, poverty and economic competition. He said the inability of many African countries to industrialise and create productive jobs had forced millions of young people into informal economic activities, where competition for limited opportunities could generate resentment. Lumumba observed that Africa’s economic dependence on exporting raw materials while importing finished products had contributed to the loss of employment opportunities to other economies. “We export crude oil and import refined petroleum. We export cocoa and import chocolate. We export minerals and import the machines, batteries and technologies manufactured from them,” he said. He added that the continent was effectively creating employment opportunities elsewhere while its young population continued to struggle for limited opportunities at home. The legal scholar said the appropriate response to the exploitation of migrant workers was to enforce labour laws against employers rather than encourage hostility towards foreigners. According to him, employers who engage undocumented migrants and pay them below lawful wages create resentment among local workers while benefiting from the division. “The appropriate response is not violence against the migrant. It is enforcement of labour law against the employer,” he said. Lumumba also highlighted the contradiction in Africans celebrating the achievements of their compatriots abroad while treating migrants from other African countries with hostility. item.title: 2027: Violence threatens turnout as party supporters come under attacks
item.description: •60 to 70 per cent of voters afraid of voting – security analyst •INEC warns of N10m fine, jail term for inflammatory campaigns •Attacks on rallies, convoys heighten fears By Omeiza Ajayi ABUJA: Between 60 to 70 per cent of Nigerian voters are afraid that political violence will stop them from voting in 2027, a security expert, Mr Onyekachi Adekoya, has said, as voter apathy continues to rise. Adekoya spoke on Friday morning on The Morning Brief, a programme on Channels Television. He cited a calculation by Yiaga Africa. “If you look at Yiaga Africa’s calculation, 60 to 70% of voters are worried that political violence will not allow them come out on the day,” he said. He said that fear works against turnout. “Once the violence and the rhetoric of it goes up, people are less likely to come out to vote, and perhaps that is, some would argue, part of the strategy at play by some parties,” he said. There have been recent incidents, including attacks on party convoys and on an assembly in some states including Delta, Cross River, Lagos, Edo and Gombe states. In Delta State, a man was apprehended and not handed over to the police. He was then reportedly killed. Adekoya said violence was already rising and would get worse. “It is already ticking over 70 incidents captured so far,” he said. “This is not the peak of it because the campaign season has just started.” He said the stakes went beyond 2027, with politicians positioning for 2031 and 2039. “We expect that this political season will be a bit more violent and true to type,” he said. He said pressure on local politicians would raise tensions. “Politicians at the local level are under significant pressure to deliver on their areas and that would most likely raise tensions. What it will look like is that politicians use violence to destabilize the opponents in opponents’ area of strength so that they can lose votes.” Adekoya said his firm’s report classed 14 states as toss-up states, which would be “keenly contested”. He named the North Central, North East and North West, and parts of the South East, as areas of concern. “Nobody should die because somebody is trying to be president,” he said. On what security agencies could do, Adekoya said the shortfall lay in resources. “If at all there is a failure in security it is because of lack of capacity, poor logistics planning and the fact that we have a hydraheaded security problem which cannot be resolved,” he said. He said enforcement could not be left to the agencies alone. “There is a command structure where also politics get in the way of enforcement. It should not be a job only for the police, it should be a collective responsibility,” he said. The concerns followed a run of threats by office holders in several states in recent weeks, which has drawn condemnation from civil society groups, rights organisations and opposition politicians. item.title: Sacking of Atiku: What Justice Lifu based his judgement on
item.description: By Luminous Jannamike ABUJA – The leadership crisis rocking the African Democratic Congress (ADC) took a decisive turn when Justice Peter Lifu of the Federal High Court, Abuja, invalidated the emergence of Senator David Mark and other executives who assumed control of the party in July 2025. But the judgment of November 5, 2026, was not simply about competing claims to party leadership. It hinged on a fundamental legal question: could the party’s National Executive Committee (NEC) use its constitutional powers to replace an existing elected leadership structure without complying with the democratic procedures prescribed by law? In the Certified True Copy (CTC) of the judgment obtained by Saturday Vanguard, Justice Lifu said he identified critical weaknesses in the defendants’ case, including the disputed resignation letter on which they relied, the limits of NEC’s administrative powers and the absence of satisfactory evidence that the new executives emerged through a democratic election. The resignation letter One of the Mark-led camp’s principal arguments was that Nafiu Bala Gombe had voluntarily resigned as Deputy National Chairman on May 17, 2025, before the NEC meeting that produced the new leadership. The letter, tendered as Exhibit ADC 1, was intended to establish that Gombe had relinquished his position and consequently lacked the legal standing to challenge the subsequent leadership transition. Justice Lifu, however, was unconvinced Rather than accept the document simply because it was certified, the judge examined its signature against Gombe’s signatures on other documents executed before a Commissioner for Oaths. He explained that certification established the status of a document as a true copy but did not, in itself, establish the authenticity of a disputed signature. After comparing the documents, he said that he found material differences in their structure, style, formation and general manner of execution. “The signatures do not appear to be one and the same,” Justice Lifu observed. He consequently described the purported resignation letter as fictitious or fabricated and rejected it as reliable evidence that Gombe had voluntarily vacated his office. The finding removed a central pillar of the defendants’ argument that Gombe had ceased to be an officer of the party before the July 2025 transition. Importantly, this was a finding made in determining the civil dispute, not a criminal conviction for forgery. NEC’s powers could not override the law The second major issue concerned the extent of NEC’s authority under Article 19(14) of the ADC constitution. The defendants maintained that the provision empowered NEC to dissolve the existing National Working Committee (NWC), make administrative arrangements and install the new executives. item.title: Women and race to 2027
item.description: Going by the number of women that have emerged candidates in the last primary elections of all the political parties in Nigeria, next year’s general polls is bound to witness fewer number of women contesting elective positions. Weekend Trust reports that while more women indicated interests in contesting by obtaining forms to secure the tickets of their parties, most of them could not go beyond the preliminary stages, with many of them either withdrawing, not considered in the consensus arrangements, or defeated in the early stages. Checks by our correspondents revealed that a higher number of women had indicated interests in contesting for state assembly seats, but the number dwindled for those going for House of Representatives seats, again, dropping drastically for Senate and getting terribly low on governorship. When the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) released the names of the presidential candidates for 2027, only two out of the 18 candidates, which constitutes 11.1per cent of the total candidates, are women, despite making up 49.32 per cent of Nigeria’s population. Amidst campaigns, Borno, Niger children remain in captivity Tinubu booed at Abuja mosque after Friday prayers They are up against 15 men, including President Bola Tinubu of the All Progressives Congress (APC), former Vice President Atiku Abubakar of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Peter Obi of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), and other candidates across the political parties. The two women are Ada Elizabeth Okwori of the National Democratic Party (NDP) and Esther Iken Okereke of the National Rescue Movement (NRM). Also, there are four female vice presidential candidates who will be contesting. These are Hajiya Bintu Konto (LP), Ofordile Peace Egobia (APP), Nafisat Usaku (DLA) and Patience Key (YPP) INEC figures obtained by Weekend Trust, showed that 469 women are among the 4,863 candidates listed for the Senate and House of Representatives elections, while only two of the 18 presidential candidates are women. The figures indicate that fewer than one in every 10 candidates contesting the National Assembly elections is female, while women constitute just over one in every 10 presidential candidates. The Senate has the lowest female representation, with 123 women among 1,303 candidates, representing 9.4 per cent. The House of Representatives has 346 female candidates out of 3,560, representing 9.7 per cent. The figures were calculated from the party and gender fields contained in INEC’s final list of candidates. The figures reflect a pattern in Nigerian politics in which women participate extensively in elections but remain largely absent from the institutions where political decisions are made. Data from 2015 show that only one woman contested the presidency, while four women were listed as vice presidential candidates, with 14 political parties participating. item.title: World Diabetes Day: High cost pushes drugs, special diets out of reach
item.description: As the world marks the 2026 World Diabetes Day today, attention is once again drawn to the importance of early diagnosis, timely treatment and sustained care in preventing complications and saving lives. But for many Nigerians living with the condition, the challenge goes beyond early detection to affording medication, special diets and regular medical checks needed to manage the disease. Some patients who spoke to Weekend Trust said the rising cost of treatment had pushed them into financial hardship, forcing them to ration prescribed drugs, compromise their diets or go for days without medication. For Mrs Ngunengen Akpam, living with diabetes has become a daily struggle, not only against the disease but also against the rising cost of managing it. Tinubu booed at Abuja mosque after Friday prayers Women and race to 2027 The burden is compounded by her responsibility to also support her diabetic mother, Mama Lydia Acka, making the cost of medication, food and routine medical care a constant source of worry for the family. Akpam told one of our correspondents that the prices of essential diabetes medications had increased considerably over the years, making it increasingly difficult to maintain the treatment prescribed by her doctors. She recalled that Metformin, one of the drugs she takes, which sold for N700 for a pack of three cards in 2015, now costs about N2,500. Similarly, Dormin, which previously sold for N700, now costs N3,500 for a pack of 10 cards, she said. “The cost of drugs has increased tremendously. I take my medication twice daily, so it is not easy. In a month, we spend so much, especially when you have another diabetic person to cater for,” she said. Medication, however, is only part of the financial burden. Akpam explained that managing diabetes also requires adherence to a carefully regulated diet, including millet, beans and vegetables, which have also become expensive. Although the price of millet had dropped from more than N1,200 to N600 per mudu during the harvest season, she said her financial circumstances still made it difficult to consistently afford the recommended food items. The experience is similar for Mrs Elahi Onu, who has lived with diabetes for 11 years and whose treatment has become a major financial responsibility for her children. Onu said her children spend at least N25,000 monthly on medication alone, while more than N60,000 goes into providing the special diet recommended for managing her condition. She listed unripe plantain, beans, vegetables, basmati rice and grains such as millet among the food items she had been advised to eat. “These special types of food are costly and drain the pockets of my children. “Sometimes there is a delay in supplies of these items to me. I will be forced to go hungry for the period or fall back to any available food,” she said. item.title: Amidst campaigns, Borno, Niger children remain in captivity
item.description: As the campaign season hots up, families of the abducted children in Borno and Niger states are still looking up to the authorities for intervention. Weekend Trust reports that while the pupils kidnapped in Borno have spent 213 days in captivity, students abducted in Niger have also remained in the hands of their captors for more than two weeks. Today makes it 213 days of agony and sleepless nights for the families of the abducted children in Mussa and Lassa communities of Askira-Uba Local Government Area in Borno State. The78 children, including toddlers less than two years old, who were abducted following two separate operations by bandits and insurgents, are still in captivity, even as politicians intensify campaigns for political power. The nightmare began on May 15, 2026 when at least 42 pupils and students were taken from their classrooms in Mussa Primary and Secondary School. Weeks later, on June 29, another set of 36 students were abducted in Government Day Secondary School, Lassa, further escalating security concerns in the area. Women and race to 2027 How IDPs built Abuja’s largest beans market Since then, the whereabouts of the children have remained unknown, plunging the families into a state of painful trauma. The Mussa school children were abducted on the same day as the 44 pupils and teachers from a school in the Oriire Local Government Area of Oyo State. But unlike the Mussa schoolchildren that have remained in captivity, the Oyo children were rescued on July 10, 2026 after 56 days in captivity after President Bola Ahmed Tinubu gave marching orders to heads of security operatives to rescue them. Weekend Trust reports that parents of the abducted pupils in Borno have on various occasions expressed frustration over what they described as “silence” from both the federal and state governments. The families are alleging that the authorities have entirely abandoned them; expressing fear that their children may have been forgotten by the same people they voted to power to protect them. The chairman of the parents of the abducted children, Mr Ishaku Suya, told our correspondent that the communities had remained in despair since the abduction of the schoolchildren. “Officially, I have not heard anything from the federal or state governments. Nobody is saying anything. And nobody has reached out to us from the side of the abductors,” he said. According to him, the mothers of the abducted children are always crying and thinking about their condition. “As men, we cannot cry, but we can’t eat food whenever we remember that our toddlers, some of them less than 2 years old, are still in the hands of their abductors. item.title: How IDPs built Abuja’s largest beans market
item.description: Ibrahim Philemon was compelled to abandon everything he had built in his youth and flee his native Gwoza for Karu in Nasarawa State because of Boko Haram’s relentless attacks on his community. Philemon is among thousands of other farmers who fled their towns because of intensified security risks posed by Boko Haram militants. But these farmers, despite facing adversity, remained undeterred. As internally displaced persons (IDPs), they were determined to rebuild their lives after the devastation caused by Boko Haram. Today, Philemon produces over 100 bags of beans and over 50 bags of maize annually since coming to Karu in 2013 as an internally displaced person. Amidst campaigns, Borno, Niger children remain in captivity Tinubu booed at Abuja mosque after Friday prayers When Boko Haram captured Gwoza town, which had an estimated population of around 388,600 in August 2014, thousands fled immediately to many states in the country and the neighbouring towns in Cameroon. Gwoza, which is located on the fringes of Sanbisa forest, is about 135 kilometres southeast of Maiduguri, the capital of Borno State. It is marked by a hilly terrain. As farmers, the displaced persons established approximately 13 camps in Karu Local Government Area of Nasarawa State, where they commenced agricultural activities. With an estimated population of over 20,000, according to the International Organisation for Migration in Nasarawa, the IDPs spread across farming communities in Karu and Keffi, seeking farmlands and clearing bushes and forests that were hitherto uncultivated to plant beans and maize. Some of them harvested over 200 bags of beans (cowpea) and maize. Within three years of their arrival, these displaced farmers rose from the ashes to establish one of the most vibrant grain markets on the outskirts of Abuja, the country’s capital, which today attracts buyers across the country. Setting up a beans market As they continued to record good harvests, selling their produce in good value immediately became a huge challenge that devastated many of them who were trying to find life after the colossal losses inflicted on them back home in Gwoza. That challenge gave birth to the establishment of what is today known as the foremost beans market in 2016, located in Auta Balefi, along the Abuja-Keffi expressway, about 25 kilometres from the Aso Rock Villa, before the National Agricultural Showground. They told our reporter, who spent a day with them, that farming and trading provided opportunities for them to rebuild their lives after displacement. David Yakubu, the secretary of the beans market, told Weekend Trust how the idea came about. He said the market was established after they encountered difficulties selling their agricultural produce at profitable prices in Ibadan, Oyo State. item.title: Emperor, 8,000 soldiers and lesson for Nigeria
item.description: I came looking for ancient soldiers and left thinking about Nigeria’s tourism potential. One thing I was particularly looking forward to during my visit to China was seeing the famous Terracotta Warriors in Xi’an. I had read about them, seen pictures, and of course, watched films inspired by the mysteries of ancient China. But nothing quite prepared me for the experience of standing in front of thousands of life-sized soldiers who have been buried underground for more than 2,000 years. And what an experience it was! If you have watched Hollywood’s The Mummy: Tomb of the Dragon Emperor, you may remember the mysterious army of clay soldiers that comes alive. Well, I finally got to see the real thing. Thankfully, none of them came alive while I was there. But standing in those enormous exhibition halls, surrounded by thousands of soldiers, horses and chariots arranged in military formation, I couldn’t help wondering what must have gone through the minds of the people who created this extraordinary army. The story takes us back to 221 BC when Qin Shi Huang became the first emperor to unify China. Like many powerful rulers of his time, he was obsessed with immortality and the idea of continuing his reign beyond death. His solution was to build an entire underground army to protect him in the afterlife. Think about that. While some people prepared for retirement, this emperor was preparing for eternity, complete with his own military formation. The scale of the project is difficult to comprehend. Thousands of life-sized clay soldiers, horses and chariots were painstakingly created. Above the excavation pit in Xi’an, I stood where visitors have looked down on the Terracotta Army for decades: thousands of figures, each made by hand, and still not fully unearthed. What makes the discovery even more fascinating is that the soldiers are not identical. They have different facial features, hairstyles, uniforms and expressions. They look like real individuals, each with a distinct identity and military rank. Then comes another remarkable twist. For over 2,000 years, this enormous army remained hidden beneath the earth until 1974 when some local farmers digging a well stumbled upon fragments of what would become one of the greatest archaeological discoveries in modern history. Imagine going out to dig a well and discovering an entire army. I wonder what the conversation was like that evening when they returned home. Today, the site is recognised globally as one of the greatest archaeological treasures in the world, and is popularly described as the Eighth Wonder of the World. The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO) designated the Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor a World Heritage Site in 1987. But beyond the fascinating history, what struck me most was what China has done with this discovery. This is where the story becomes particularly interesting for Nigeria.
